lesson_title: Contour Lines: Reading the Shape of the Land
hook_text: These squiggly lines are a 3D mountain — once you know the code.
clip_script: Now the single most useful sentence in mapwork: the closer together the contour lines, the steeper the slope; the further apart, the gentler the slope. Why must this be true? Reason it out — do not memorise it. Between any two neighbouring contours the land climbs exactly 20 metres; that is fixed by the interval. What varies is the horizontal distance you walk to gain those 20 metres. If the lines sit a kilometre apart on the map, you stroll a kilometre to rise 20 metres — a gentle slope. If the lines crowd within 100 metres of each other, you gain the same 20 metres in a tenth of the walking distance — a demanding climb. Same rise, shorter run, steeper gradient.
visual_style: Flat contour map morphing into a rotating 3D terrain model, lines lighting up as the slope steepens.
pacing: Slow reveal of the morph, then brisk through the reasoning, landing hard on 'same rise, shorter run'.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find the valley, the cliff and the summit yourself.
